chapter_summary:
Virtualization and containerization technologies are fundamental to modern Linux infrastructure, but they introduce new layers of complexity for troubleshooting. For traditional virtualization, like KVM/QEMU managed by `libvirt`, issues can arise at the host level, the guest level, or in the interaction between them. Common KVM/QEMU problems include VMs failing to start, network connectivity issues within guests, or storage performance bottlenecks. When a VM fails to start, check the `libvirt` logs, typically found in `/var/log/libvirt/qemu/<vm_name>.log` or accessible via `journalctl -u libvirtd`. These logs often pinpoint issues with disk image access, network bridge configuration, or insufficient host resources. `virsh list --all` shows the status of all VMs, and `virsh console <vm_name>` can provide direct console access to a non-booting guest, much like a physical server.

Network troubleshooting for VMs often involves verifying the host's bridge configuration (e.g., `br0` created by `virsh net-start default`). Use `brctl show` or `ip link show` on the host to inspect the bridge and its attached interfaces. Ensure the guest's virtual network interface is correctly attached to the bridge. Storage issues can stem from corrupted QCOW2 images, insufficient space on the host, or performance contention if multiple VMs share the same underlying storage. `qemu-img info <image_path>` provides details about the virtual disk image. A common mistake is to overlook host resource exhaustion; if the host runs out of CPU, memory, or disk I/O, all its guests will suffer. Monitoring host resources with `top`, `free`, `iostat` (as discussed in Chapter 11.5) is crucial for diagnosing guest performance problems.

Containerization, primarily with Docker, presents a different set of diagnostic challenges. When a Docker container fails to start or exits unexpectedly, the first place to look is its logs: `docker logs <container_id_or_name>`. These logs often contain application-specific errors or messages indicating why the container exited. `docker inspect <container_id_or_name>` provides a wealth of metadata about the container, including its configuration, network settings, and exit code. A non-zero exit code usually indicates an application error. Common Docker issues include incorrect `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` in the `Dockerfile`, missing environment variables, port conflicts, or permission issues within the container (e.g., the application trying to write to a non-writable path). `docker exec -it <container_id> bash` allows you to shell into a running container to inspect its filesystem, processes, and network configuration, which is invaluable for debugging.

For Kubernetes, the complexity scales significantly. Pod failures are common and require a systematic approach. `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows pod status and node assignment. `kubectl describe pod <pod_name>` provides detailed information, including events, container statuses, and reasons for failure (e.g., `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff`, `OOMKilled`). `kubectl logs <pod_name> -c <container_name>` retrieves container logs. `CrashLoopBackOff` is a frequent status, meaning the container is repeatedly starting and crashing; examining its logs is paramount. Network issues in Kubernetes can involve `Service` discovery, `Ingress` routing, or `CNI` (Container Network Interface) problems. `kubectl get svc`, `kubectl get ing`, and `kubectl describe svc <service_name>` help diagnose service-level connectivity. If a pod cannot reach another service, check `kube-proxy` logs on the node or the `CNI` plugin logs. Resource limits (`requests` and `limits` in Pod specs) can also cause `OOMKilled` (Out Of Memory Killed) errors if a container exceeds its memory limit, or CPU throttling if it exceeds its CPU limit. Understanding the interaction between pods, nodes, services, and the underlying network is key to effective Kubernetes troubleshooting.

screens.title: Virtualization & Containerization Diagnostics
screens.subtitle: Systematic troubleshooting across KVM/QEMU, Docker, and Kubernetes

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn a systematic, layered approach to diagnosing virtualization and containerization failures. You will develop habits that separate host-level failures from guest or container problems, interpret the most useful logs and command outputs, and apply quick fixes that are safe for production. For KVM and QEMU, we focus on libvirt and virsh commands, reading VM logs, and checking network bridges and virtual disks. For containers, we'll walk through reading docker logs, inspecting metadata, and using an interactive shell to inspect runtime state. For Kubernetes, you'll learn a clear triage flow: pod status, describe output, container logs, and then service and CNI checks. Each method pairs a definition with a concrete example and a common misconception to avoid. For instance, rapid VM reboots are often blamed on the guest OS, but host resource starvation is a common cause. By the end of this lesson you will be able to trace a failure from symptom to root cause using focused commands and measurements. Think of this chapter as a debugging checklist you can use under pressure: capture the right logs, verify the networking and storage layers, and confirm resource limits before applying changes.

keyIdea.title: Layered Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Always separate host, hypervisor, and guest/container layers; inspect logs and resource metrics at each layer before changing configurations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll practice and why they matter

narration.text: These objectives set a clear path for troubleshooting across virtualization and container stacks. First, you will learn to diagnose common KVM and QEMU failures by reading libvirt logs and using virsh commands to inspect VM state and consoles. This is vital because VM boots often fail for reasons that are logged but not obvious from the guest's perspective. Second, you'll practice troubleshooting network and storage connectivity for guests, verifying bridges, interfaces, and virtual disk integrity so you can separate network misconfiguration from storage corruption. Third, you'll learn Docker debugging: reading container logs, using inspect to view runtime metadata, and entering running containers to check file permissions and processes. Those skills let you resolve misconfigured entrypoints, missing environment variables, or permission failures. Fourth, you'll debug Kubernetes pod failures and service connectivity by using kubectl get, describe, and logs, and by interpreting statuses like CrashLoopBackOff and OOMKilled. Each objective emphasizes a hands-on command or check you will use under pressure, and together they let you triage from symptom to root cause with confidence.

keyIdea.text: Master a small set of host, container, and cluster commands to quickly identify where a failure originates.

screens.title: KVM/QEMU basics and common VM failures
screens.subtitle: Why VMs fail to start and where to look first

narration.text: When a VM fails to start, you need a principled first check to avoid guessing. libvirt centralizes virtualization management for KVM/QEMU; its logs often tell you why a domain won't boot. Start by confirming VM existence and state with the command that lists all domains. If the VM shows as shut off or in an error state, inspect the QEMU domain log typically stored under the libvirt log directory or use the system journal for the libvirt service. These logs reveal disk image access errors, xml configuration issues, missing devices, or permission problems. A concrete example: a VM that cannot open its QCOW2 image will show input and output errors in the qemu log, which points you to the disk path, SELinux denial, or missing backing file. A frequent misconception is to immediately reinstall the guest OS; often the guest kernel is fine but the host cannot provide the backing storage or a bridged network interface. Key checks you will use every time are: list domains, open a console to observe boot messages when possible, read the libvirt/qemu log for tracebacks, and verify host file permissions and available disk space. Practice these steps until they are second nature; they dramatically shorten time-to-fix for VM boot failures.

keyIdea.title: Start with libvirt logs
keyIdea.text: Libvirt/QEMU logs and domain listings show the direct cause of boot failures more often than guessing at guest-level corruption.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › KVM/QEMU Start Failures
Definition

A VM start failure means the hypervisor did not hand control to the guest kernel; the root cause can be host resources, missing images, device mapping errors, or libvirt configuration problems.

Common checks
  • Use virsh list --all to see domain state and IDs.
  • Read /var/log/libvirt/qemu/<vm_name>.log or journalctl -u libvirtd for errors.
  • Use virsh console <vm_name> for direct boot messages on non-graphical guests.
  • Verify disk paths, permissions, and backing files with qemu-img info.
Key Takeaway

Always read the libvirt/qemu logs before making configuration changes to the guest; they point to the failing subsystem.

Concrete Example
# Inspect domains and logs
virsh list --all
journalctl -u libvirtd --since "1 hour ago"
# Check QEMU log
cat /var/log/libvirt/qemu/webserver-vm.log
Common misconception

Assuming the guest OS is corrupted. Often the host cannot access the disk image or lacks permissions; logs show that clearly.

screens.title: Inspecting libvirt and virsh for VM state
screens.subtitle: Commands to confirm domain state, console access, and log locations

narration.text: When you suspect a VM-level problem, follow a short process to gather reliable data before changing anything. Step one: list domains to confirm which VMs exist and their current state. This reveals if a VM is running, paused, or shut off. Step two: if the VM exists but will not boot, open a console session to observe kernel messages or early boot failures; that can show file-system checks or init errors. Step three: read the QEMU domain log under libvirt or view the libvirtd system journal to capture permission denials, xml parsing errors, or device attach failures. Step four: inspect virtual interfaces and disks declared in the domain XML; incorrect paths or typos are common. A concrete command sequence is: list domains, console to watch boot, then read the specific qemu log for that VM. A common misconception is to rely solely on virsh start/stop results. Those commands indicate transitions but not why they failed. The logs provide the why. End by asking: what specific error in the QEMU log points to disk access, network bridge, or device mapping? That targeted question focuses your next action.

keyIdea.title: Short data-gather process
keyIdea.text: List, console, and read the domain log; the sequence gives state, live boot output, and detailed failures.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › virsh & libvirt Process
Process Steps
  1. Step 1: virsh list --all — confirm domain presence and state.
  2. Step 2: virsh console <vm_name> — observe boot messages for kernel or init failures.
  3. Step 3: journalctl -u libvirtd or /var/log/libvirt/qemu/<vm_name>.log — read error traces.
  4. Step 4: Inspect domain XML for interface and disk declarations if logs indicate device problems.
Examples & Commands
virsh list --all
virsh console webserver-vm
journalctl -u libvirtd --since "30 minutes ago"
cat /var/log/libvirt/qemu/webserver-vm.log
Misconception

Seeing a domain listed as running doesn't guarantee guest network or disk access; use console and logs to validate runtime behavior.

screens.title: VM networking: bridge checks vs guest interface issues
screens.subtitle: Separate host bridge faults from guest network misconfiguration

narration.text: Network failures that appear inside a VM can originate on the host bridge or inside the guest interface. To avoid false assumptions, compare the host bridge state with the guest interface presence. On the host, commands to show bridges and attached interfaces will reveal whether the expected tap device or bridge exists and is up. If the host bridge lacks the VM tap device, the guest cannot reach the network regardless of its internal configuration. Inside the guest, check IP addresses, routes, and interface states to confirm that DHCP or static assignment succeeded. A concrete diagnostic flow: run a host bridge show, verify the tap on the bridge, then attempt to ping the guest IP from the host. If ping fails but the tap is present, open the guest console and examine ip addr show and ip route. A common misconception is to restart the guest firewall first; often the problem is the bridge name changed or a missing attachment after a host update. The key diagnostic separation is: if the host bridge shows no tap, fix the host; if the tap exists but the guest lacks an IP, fix guest networking or DHCP.

keyIdea.title: Host vs Guest Network
keyIdea.text: Confirm the host bridge and tap devices exist before modifying guest network settings or firewalls.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › VM Networking
Host Bridge Checks
  • Use brctl show or ip link show to list bridges and attached interfaces.
  • Confirm the VM's tap device is present and UP on the expected bridge (e.g., virbr0 or br0).
  • Ping the guest IP from the host to verify L2/L3 connectivity.
# On host
brctl show
ip link show br0
ip addr show
Guest Interface Checks
  • Use ip addr show and ip route to confirm the guest has an IP and default route.
  • Check DHCP client logs if the guest should receive an address automatically.
  • If the tap exists but no IP is present, focus on guest network config rather than the host bridge.
# In guest
ip addr show
ip route show
journalctl -u dhclient
Common mistake

Restarting the guest firewall before checking the host bridge can waste time if the tap device is missing on the host.

screens.title: VM storage issues and qemu-img
screens.subtitle: Detect corrupted images, missing backing files, and host disk exhaustion

narration.text: Virtual disks introduce a distinct failure mode for virtual machines. QCOW2 images may have backings, snapshots, or corrupt sectors that prevent a VM from starting or cause performance degradation. The qemu-img tool provides a concise view of image format, virtual size, backing file, and whether the image is read-only. Use it to check for unexpected backing files or inconsistencies. If the host lacks free space on the filesystem containing the images, guests will fail to write and may crash or exhibit corruption. Performance issues can also appear when multiple VMs share a single physical disk under heavy input and output; the symptom is high latency within guests, not necessarily an immediate error message. A concrete command is qemu-img info on the image path; follow this by checking host disk usage and input and output statistics with tools you already know. A common misconception is to assume guest-level fsck will solve all disk errors. If the underlying image is inaccessible or truncated on the host, guest fsck cannot fix host-level corruption. The correct sequence is to validate the host image health, then mount or attach read-only copies for guest repairs if necessary.

keyIdea.title: Check image metadata
keyIdea.text: qemu-img info shows backing files and sizes; combine with host disk and I/O checks to diagnose storage-caused guest failures.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › VM Storage
Checks for virtual disks
  • Run qemu-img info <image_path> to view format, virtual size, and backing file.
  • Confirm the host filesystem has sufficient free space where images reside.
  • Use iostat or similar to detect high disk latency from competing VMs.
qemu-img info /var/lib/libvirt/images/webserver.qcow2
df -h /var/lib/libvirt/images
iostat -x 1 5
Example scenario

A VM experiences frequent timeouts accessing disk-backed databases. qemu-img shows a backing file on shared storage and iostat indicates high await times. The correct fix is to move high-I/O guests to less contended storage or add IOPS, rather than spending time tuning guest filesystem caches alone.

Pro tip

If an image has a backing file, never delete the backing without rebasing; that causes immediate corruption for derived images.

screens.title: Docker container diagnostics: logs, inspect, and exec
screens.subtitle: Find why a container exits and how to investigate running state

narration.text: Docker containers can fail for many application-level reasons, but the container runtime gives you immediate evidence: logs, metadata, and an interactive shell. Start with docker ps -a to find containers and their exit statuses. A non-zero exit code usually means the process inside failed; docker logs shows the application output that led to termination. docker inspect provides JSON metadata including configured entrypoint, command, environment variables, mount points, and network settings; this is often where misconfiguration is exposed. If a container is running but misbehaving, use docker exec -it to start a shell and inspect file permissions, running processes, and environment. A concrete example: a web app container exits immediately with a missing binary message; docker inspect shows an incorrect CMD in the image, and rebuilding with the correct ENTRYPOINT fixes the lifecycle. A common misconception is to assume docker restart will fix config problems; restart simply reruns the same faulty configuration. Instead, inspect the container metadata and logs to identify whether the issue is entrypoint, env, port conflict, or permission. Closing question: after seeing an exit code, what two sources will you inspect first to find the cause?

keyIdea.title: Logs + Inspect
keyIdea.text: Docker logs explain runtime failure; docker inspect shows the declared configuration that often causes the failure.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Docker Diagnostics
Essential Commands
docker ps -a
docker logs my-failing-app
docker inspect my-failing-app
docker exec -it my-running-app /bin/bash
  • Use logs first for application errors.
  • Use inspect to validate CMD, ENTRYPOINT, and mounts.
  • Use exec to validate runtime permissions and processes.
Example: failing image
# Dockerfile causing failure
FROM alpine/git
CMD ["non_existent_command"]

This Dockerfile will cause an immediate exit. After docker run, docker ps -a shows the container as exited, docker logs will include the shell error, and docker inspect reveals the CMD. Correcting the CMD and rebuilding resolves the lifecycle issue.

Check your assumption

Don't assume a missing file inside the image is the runtime issue until you inspect the image's declared CMD and mounted volumes.

screens.title: Hands-on: build, fail, and fix a Docker image
screens.subtitle: Walk through the failing Dockerfile, inspect logs, and correct the CMD

narration.text: We'll walk through a small hands-on scenario to practice the docker debugging flow. First, build the intentionally failing Dockerfile that uses a non-existent command; this simulates an image with a bad entrypoint. Next, run the image and observe the exited container with docker ps -a. Inspect the logs to see the shell error that terminated the process and use docker inspect to confirm the declared CMD and entrypoint. Then fix the Dockerfile by replacing the failing command with a simple, known-good command, rebuild, and rerun to verify success. The important learning point is the sequence: build, run, inspect exit, read logs, inspect metadata, enter a running container when available. A common misconception to avoid is editing a running container to 'fix' the image; changes inside a running container do not update the image you would redeploy. Instead, update the Dockerfile, rebuild, and redeploy immutable artifacts. Practice this flow until each step becomes automatic under time pressure. Hands-on: build, fail, and fix a Docker image means fix the source dockerfile and rebuild images rather than editing running containers when correcting entrypoint or environment issues.. In practical terms, walk through the failing dockerfile, inspect logs, and correct the cmd. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Immutable fix pattern
keyIdea.text: Fix the source Dockerfile and rebuild images rather than editing running containers when correcting entrypoint or environment issues.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Docker Lab
Failing Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM alpine/git
CMD ["non_existent_command"]
Build and run to see the exit status, then collect logs and inspect metadata before changing the Dockerfile.
Fix and verify
# Fix: replace the CMD with a known binary
# Dockerfile (fixed)
FROM alpine/git
CMD ["echo", "Hello from Docker!"]

# Commands to verify
docker build -t failing-app .
docker run --name my-failing-app failing-app
docker logs my-failing-app
Remember: rebuild the image, then run the new image. Editing a running container does not update the source artifact used in deployments.

screens.title: Kubernetes pod triage: get, describe, and logs
screens.subtitle: A systematic approach to interpret pod status and events

narration.text: Kubernetes adds orchestration complexity, so you need a short triage routine for pod failures. Start with kubectl get pods -o wide to see pod status, node assignment, and restart counts. If a pod is not running, kubectl describe pod gives events and last state reasons such as ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, or OOMKilled. Always collect container logs with kubectl logs; include the container name when the pod has multiple containers. For CrashLoopBackOff, logs usually show why the container exits repeatedly. For ImagePullBackOff, describe events identify registry errors or authentication failures. A concrete example: a pod in CrashLoopBackOff will show a short-lived container exit; kubectl logs reveals an application stack trace, and describe shows repeated restarts. A common misconception is to delete and recreate the pod without reviewing events; that wastes time if the image name is wrong or a secret is missing. End each triage by asking: does the evidence point to an image, an internal application error, a resource limit, or network/registry access? That guides whether to fix the manifest, the image, or node-level issues. Kubernetes pod triage: get, describe, and logs means use get, describe, and logs in that order to interpret pod state, events, and container output before making changes.. In practical terms, a systematic approach to interpret pod status and events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Triaging pods
keyIdea.text: Use get, describe, and logs in that order to interpret pod state, events, and container output before making changes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Kubernetes Triage
Essential kubectl flow
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod failing-pod
kubectl logs failing-pod -c container-name
  • Use get to locate the pod and node assignment.
  • Use describe to read events, last state and reason strings.
  • Use logs to see application-level errors causing restarts.
Example: CrashLoopBackOff

A pod with CrashLoopBackOff will restart repeatedly. Describe shows the restart count and last termination reason, while logs reveal the application error. If logs show out-of-memory, check resource requests and limits in the manifest.

Misconception

Deleting a crashing pod without fixing the root cause simply recreates the same error; find the cause via logs and events first.

screens.title: Network and service connectivity in Kubernetes
screens.subtitle: Diagnose Service, Ingress, kube-proxy, and CNI issues

narration.text: Networking in Kubernetes spans many layers: Services, kube-proxy, CNI plugins, and node networking. When a pod cannot reach a service, begin by confirming the Service object exists and targets the expected pods using kubectl get svc and kubectl describe svc. Next, verify endpoints are populated; an empty endpoint list indicates the service selectors do not match pod labels. If endpoints look correct but traffic still fails, examine kube-proxy logs on the node for iptables or IPVS programming errors and check the CNI plugin logs for overlay network failures. For Ingress issues, validate that the Ingress resource matches the controller and that the controller's logs show accepted routes. A concrete diagnostic sequence: kubectl get svc, kubectl describe svc to confirm endpoints, ssh to the node to view kube-proxy logs, and check CNI daemon logs for errors. A common misconception is to assume DNS in the cluster is at fault; while DNS can break, many connectivity problems are due to missing endpoints or CNI disruptions. The takeaway is to treat Services and endpoints as the first layer of truth and then inspect node-level networking components if endpoints are present but connectivity fails.

keyIdea.title: Services → Endpoints → Node
keyIdea.text: Verify that Services have matching endpoints before investigating node-level kube-proxy or CNI logs for routing failures.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Kubernetes Networking
Service & Endpoint checks
kubectl get svc
kubectl describe svc my-service
kubectl get endpoints my-service
If endpoints are empty, the Service selector doesn't match pods. Fix labels or selector in the manifest rather than tinkering with kube-proxy.
Node-level checks
  • Check kube-proxy logs on the node for iptables or IPVS errors.
  • Inspect the CNI plugin daemon logs when pod-to-pod networking or overlay issues appear.
  • For Ingress, verify the controller logs and resource mapping.
Pro tip

Confirm endpoints first; it often saves hours of node-level debugging.

screens.title: Resource limits, OOMKilled and performance isolation
screens.subtitle: How requests and limits affect container behavior and host performance

narration.text: Resource configuration in containers and Kubernetes greatly influences runtime stability. In Kubernetes, specifying requests and limits controls scheduler decisions and runtime cgroup constraints. If a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel will terminate it with OOMKilled; the pod status and describe output show that reason. C P U throttling happens when a container exceeds its C P U limit, producing performance degradation without explicit termination. For VMs, host-level exhaustion of C P U, memory, or input and output affects every guest; symptoms are slow responses, timeouts, or application-level errors rather than clear exit codes. A practical example: a microservice repeatedly crashes under load; kubectl describe shows OOMKilled and logs show memory allocation failure. The fix is to adjust limits or optimize memory usage and, if the node lacks capacity, move workloads or increase node resources. A misconception is to set very large limits for every pod; that risks host overcommit and noisy-neighbor effects. The guiding rule is to match limits to observed usage and scale the cluster or storage to provide isolation without over-allocation. Resource limits, OOMKilled and performance isolation means use requests and limits guided by metrics; mismatches lead to oomkilled or host-level performance problems.. In practical terms, how requests and limits affect container behavior and host performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match limits to usage
keyIdea.text: Use requests and limits guided by metrics; mismatches lead to OOMKilled or host-level performance problems.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Resources & Limits
Kubernetes resource signals
  • OOMKilled indicates the container exceeded its memory limit and was terminated.
  • CPU throttling reduces compute performance when limits are hit; no explicit termination occurs.
  • Describe output includes termination reason and exit codes to confirm resource-related kills.
Practical steps
  1. Check pod usage and limits in the manifest.
  2. If OOMKilled, increase memory limit or optimize the app's memory footprint.
  3. If the node is saturated, scale or move workloads to balance I/O and CPU.
Key Takeaway

Tune requests and limits based on observed metrics to prevent terminations and noisy neighbors on shared hosts.

screens.title: Lab scenario: diagnose failing Docker container and CrashLoopBackOff pod
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step tasks to reproduce, observe, and fix both failures

narration.text: In this lab scenario you'll apply the earlier checks to two related failures: a Docker container that fails to start and a Kubernetes pod in CrashLoopBackOff. For the Docker task, build the provided failing Dockerfile, run it to observe the exited container, collect docker ps -a, docker logs, and docker inspect. Fix the Dockerfile by replacing the non-existent command with a simple command, rebuild, and run to confirm success. For the Kubernetes task, apply the failing pod manifest that sleeps briefly and exits with an error to simulate CrashLoopBackOff. Use kubectl get pods to observe the status, kubectl describe pod to read events and last state, and kubectl logs to see the container output. Fix the pod manifest by providing a long-running command such as running the actual service process or adjusting args to keep the container alive, then reapply and confirm the pod reaches Running. A common mistake is to edit the local deployment without checking events; always read describe events first. This activity trains you to collect the right evidence before changing manifests and to prefer immutable fixes (rebuild or reapply) rather than in-place changes on running containers.

keyIdea.title: Collect evidence, then fix
keyIdea.text: Reproduce failures, collect logs and describe output, then apply immutable fixes: rebuild images or reapply corrected manifests.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Lab: Docker & Kubernetes
Docker task
# Build and run
docker build -t failing-app .
docker run --name my-failing-app failing-app
# Diagnose
docker ps -a
docker logs my-failing-app
docker inspect my-failing-app
Fix the Dockerfile and rebuild the image; do not edit the container for persistent fixes.
Kubernetes task
# Failing pod manifest snippet
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: failing-nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx-container
    image: nginx:latest
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args: ["sleep 5; exit 1"]

# Diagnose
kubectl apply -f failing-pod.yaml
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod failing-nginx
kubectl logs failing-nginx
Fix by providing a proper long-running command (for nginx, use the standard nginx foreground args) and reapply.

narration.text: Keep a short mental checklist when troubleshooting: start with scope—host or guest—then collect logs and runtime metadata, and finally validate networking and storage. For KVM/QEMU, libvirt centralizes logs and virsh is the primary control plane; read the QEMU domain logs and use virsh console to observe boot-time messages. For Docker, container logs and docker inspect are the most direct evidence of lifecycle problems; use docker exec to inspect the runtime when containers are healthy. These concepts are not independent: resource exhaustion on the host can make containers and VMs appear flaky, so always check host metrics when symptoms are broad. A good rule is to collect the minimal evidence to decide whether to rebuild, reconfigure, or migrate workloads. This short checklist reduces downtime and avoids unnecessary changes. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Short checklist
keyIdea.text: Scope → Logs → Inspect → Fix: use this sequence for reliable troubleshooting across hypervisors and containers.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Key Concepts
KVM/QEMU
Hypervisor layer; use libvirt logs and virsh for domain control and diagnostics.
libvirt / virsh
Management interface; virsh list, console and logs reveal VM state and boot errors.
Docker
Container runtime; docker logs, inspect and exec are primary diagnostic tools.
Summary
A short, repeatable checklist reduces firefighting time: determine scope, collect logs, inspect metadata, then apply immutable fixes or resource adjustments.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Commands, statuses, and common errors to keep in mind

narration.text: Remember a handful of commands and status meanings that appear frequently in incidents. For VMs: virsh list --all, virsh domiflist, virsh console, and journalctl or libvirt qemu logs. For containers: docker ps -a, docker logs, docker inspect, and docker exec. For Kubernetes: kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod, and kubectl logs. Learn the common pod statuses: ImagePullBackOff indicates an image pull failure, CrashLoopBackOff means a container repeatedly crashes, and OOMKilled indicates a memory limit termination. Use these status strings as precise signals that guide your next command. Finally, always check host resource metrics when many guests or pods show degraded performance; an exhausted host is a frequent root cause. Keep this compact map of commands and meanings handy as your first line of defense when services fail. What to Remember means associate a short command set with each technology and treat status strings as clues that narrow your investigation path.. In practical terms, commands, statuses, and common errors to keep in mind. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Commands & Statuses
keyIdea.text: Associate a short command set with each technology and treat status strings as clues that narrow your investigation path.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Quick Reference
Kubernetes
kubectl get/describe/logs. Watch for CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled.
Docker
docker ps, logs, inspect, exec to find exit codes and configuration errors.
KVM / libvirt
virsh list/console/domiflist and libvirt/qemu logs are your direct source for VM boot and device errors.
Final Tip
Treat status strings and log errors as precise signals. Let them tell you whether to check images, manifests, host resources, or CNI components next.
